lesson.text: Quick memory: how many hours of sleep do children your age need? (About 9 to 12.) Good sleep helps your body fight germs too.
Germs are living things far too small to see without a microscope. Most are harmless, but some can make you ill, like the germs that give you a cold or an upset tummy.
Germs spread on hands, in the tiny drops from coughs and sneezes, and on food and things we touch. They cannot walk or fly by themselves: they travel on us!
Catch it, bin it, kill it: sneeze into a tissue (or into your elbow), put the tissue in a bin, then wash your hands.

picture.title: Catch it, bin it, kill it

lesson.text: Wash your hands with soap and warm water for about 20 seconds, as long as singing 'Happy Birthday' twice: palms, backs, between the fingers, thumbs and nails. Rinse, then dry.
Wash your hands after the toilet and before you eat or cook. Wash them after touching animals, after blowing your nose, and when you come in from playing.
Look after your teeth: brush twice a day for about 2 minutes, last thing at night and one other time, with fluoride toothpaste. Spit the toothpaste out, but do not rinse. Have sugary food less often.
Try it in the world: build a hand-washing station by your farm, with water and a sign showing the steps and '20 seconds'. Then wash your real hands and count to 20!

exercises.prompt: How long should you wash your hands with soap?
exercises.hint: How long does 'Happy Birthday' take, sung twice?
exercises.explain: About 20 seconds: as long as singing 'Happy Birthday' twice.

exercises.prompt: Germs are too small to see with just your eyes.
exercises.hint: What would you need to see them?
exercises.explain: True: germs are so small you need a microscope to see them.

exercises.prompt: When must you wash your hands?
exercises.hint: Germs can be on hands that look clean.
exercises.explain: After the toilet, before eating or cooking, after animals, after blowing your nose, and after playing.

exercises.prompt: How many times a day should you brush your teeth?
exercises.hint: Last thing at night and one other time.
exercises.explain: Twice a day: last thing at night and one other time.

exercises.hint: You need wet hands before the soap.
items: rub palms, backs, fingers and thumbs
exercises.explain: Wet, add soap, rub every part for about 20 seconds, rinse, then dry.

exercises.prompt: What does 'catch it, bin it, kill it' mean?
exercises.hint: It is about coughs and sneezes.
choices: sneeze into a tissue, bin it, wash your hands
catch a ball and throw it away
put your hands in the bin
exercises.explain: Catch the sneeze in a tissue, put the tissue in a bin, and wash your hands to kill the germs.

exercises.prompt: For about how long should you brush your teeth each time?
exercises.hint: Long enough to clean every tooth, front and back.
exercises.explain: About 2 minutes each time, cleaning every tooth.

exercises.prompt: Does it spread germs, or stop them?
exercises.hint: Think of how germs travel from one person to another.
exercises.explain: Spreads: sneezing into hands, sharing a bottle, dirty hands on food. Stops: soap, a tissue, coughing into your elbow.

exercises.prompt: Water on its own gets rid of germs as well as soap and water.
exercises.explain: False: soap lifts germs off your skin so the water can wash them away.

exercises.prompt: Zara is going to make sandwiches after stroking the dog. What should she do first?
exercises.hint: Animals can carry germs on their fur.
choices: dry her hands on the dog
wipe her hands on her top
exercises.explain: Wash her hands with soap and water, so no germs from the dog get onto the food.

exercises.prompt: Why sneeze into your elbow rather than into your hand?
exercises.hint: What would your hand touch next?
choices: you touch things with your hands, not your elbow
exercises.explain: Your hands touch door handles, food and people, spreading germs; your elbow does not.

exercises.prompt: Why spit out toothpaste but not rinse your mouth with water?
choices: the fluoride stays to protect your teeth
exercises.explain: Not rinsing leaves the fluoride on your teeth, where it keeps protecting them.

exercises.prompt: Germs can spread in the tiny drops from a sneeze.
exercises.hint: What comes out of your nose when you sneeze?
exercises.explain: True: a sneeze sprays tiny drops that can carry germs to other people.

exercises.prompt: Match each germ-stopper to what it does.
exercises.hint: Think of each one in the lesson.
exercises.explain: Soap washes germs off your skin, a tissue catches a sneeze, a toothbrush cleans your teeth, a bin takes used tissues away.

exercises.prompt: Mimi brushes her teeth for 2 minutes, twice a day. How many minutes is that each day?
Each hand wash takes about 20 seconds. Mimi washes her hands 6 times today. How many seconds is that?
exercises.hint: Multiply the washes by the seconds for each one.
exercises.explain: 6 × 20 = 120 seconds, which is 2 minutes in a whole day: a small time to keep germs away.
